paragraphs.heading: A chain of reactions
paragraphs.text: A metabolic pathway is a chain of chemical reactions that happen one after another inside a cell. The molecules involved, whether starting materials, in-between forms or end products, are called metabolites. Enzymes drive each step, and usually what one enzyme makes becomes the starting material, or substrate, of the next. Side products are treated as waste and removed from the cell.

paragraphs.heading: Building up and breaking down
paragraphs.text: Pathways come in two main kinds. Anabolic pathways spend energy to build molecules, joining smaller ones into larger, more complex ones. Catabolic pathways break complex molecules apart and release energy as they go. The two fit together, because the energy freed by breaking down pays for the building up. A third kind, the amphibolic pathway, can work either way, depending on how much energy is needed or available.

paragraphs.heading: Paying for the work
paragraphs.text: Catabolic pathways store the energy they release in carrier molecules. They add a high-energy phosphate bond to ADP and GDP, making ATP and GTP, and they also make carriers such as NADH and NADPH from carbohydrates, fats and proteins. Their end products are often carbon dioxide, water and ammonia. Anabolic pathways, which build things like proteins, nucleic acids and lipids, are unfavorable on their own, because their reactions have a positive Gibbs free energy (+ΔG). They need to be coupled to an exergonic reaction that supplies chemical energy.

paragraphs.heading: Mostly one-way streets
paragraphs.text: Pathways are usually thought of as running in one direction. Every chemical reaction can in principle go backwards, but conditions in the cell often make one direction more favorable. So a cell may build an amino acid by one pathway and break it down by a separate one. Some steps are locked: as glucose enters a cell, ATP at once adds a phosphate to it, making glucose 6-phosphate in an irreversible first step.

paragraphs.heading: Glucose, the exception
paragraphs.text: Glucose handling bends this rule. Glycolysis breaks glucose down, yet several of its reactions can reverse and help rebuild glucose, a process called gluconeogenesis. This happens in the liver, and sometimes in the kidney, to keep blood glucose at the right level and supply the brain and muscles. It is not a perfect mirror of glycolysis: four of its enzymes are different, and they let it proceed spontaneously. When fats or proteins are plentiful, parts of glycolysis can also run backward to make glucose 6-phosphate for storage as glycogen or starch.

paragraphs.heading: Place and control
paragraphs.text: Inside a eukaryotic cell, different pathways happen in different places. The electron transport chain and oxidative phosphorylation run in the mitochondrial membrane, while glycolysis, the pentose phosphate pathway and fatty acid synthesis take place in the cytosol. Building and breaking-down pathways are often kept apart, either in separate organelles or by needing different enzymes and co-factors. Cells tune how much material flows through each pathway to their needs and to the supply of substrate, which helps keep an organism in balance. Many pathways are also regulated by feedback inhibition.

paragraphs.heading: Shared by all life
paragraphs.text: A core set of energy-producing catabolic pathways is found, in some form, in every living thing. All cells can carry out anaerobic respiration through glycolysis. Most organisms can also use the more efficient aerobic respiration of the citric acid cycle and oxidative phosphorylation. Plants, algae and cyanobacteria go further, using sunlight to build compounds from non-living matter by photosynthesis.
